Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Vanguard Electric Vehicles Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question at that time, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star then two. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Chen, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Chen:
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Vanguard Electric Vehicles' Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Elena Vasquez, CEO; Michael Reyes, CFO; Raj Singh, Chief Manufacturing Officer; and Dr. Lisa Novak, Chief Technology Officer; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Elena Vasquez.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Q3 was a significant quarter for Vanguard Electric Vehicles, marked by progress across our key strategic initiatives. We achieved notable milestones in record vehicle deliveries totaling over half a million units, substantial year-over-year revenue growth driven by our automotive and energy segments, sharp declines in battery costs per kilowatt-hour through scale and innovation, resilience against raw material cost pressures and supply chain disruptions via hedging and localization, robust delivery volumes across models and regions with balanced geographic expansion, and effective pricing strategies coupled with targeted promotions that boosted demand while protecting margins. We are particularly pleased with the initial customer response to our Vanguard Pulse hatchback, and its rapid ramp-up has had a substantial impact on our backlog, now standing at over 420,000 units.

These results validate our ecosystem flywheel: scaling deliveries funds battery advancements, which lower costs and enable energy storage growth, creating a virtuous cycle that positions us for leadership in the EV megatrend. Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Reyes to discuss our financial performance in more detail.

Michael Reyes:
Thank you, Elena. Good morning, everyone. For Q3 2024, our total revenue reached $28.4 billion, demonstrating a robust 32% increase compared to the same period last year, up from $21.5 billion in Q3 2023. This not only exceeded our guidance midpoint of $27.0 to $28.0 billion but also beat consensus estimates by about 5%. On a constant currency basis, growth was even stronger at 34%, highlighting the underlying strength of our operations despite foreign exchange headwinds in Europe.

Our gross margin stood at 21.5%, reflecting our commitment to operational excellence and cost discipline. Automotive gross margins expanded 450 basis points year-over-year, driven by sequential cost reductions in our 4680 battery cells. Operating expenses amounted to $6.2 billion, including heavy investments in R&D and factory expansions, while net income came in at $2.8 billion. We maintain a robust financial position with $18.5 billion in cash and cash equivalents, providing ample liquidity for growth initiatives.

Let me break down the revenue by core streams for a clearer view of the drivers. Automotive revenue, which accounted for 82% of total at $23.3 billion, surged 38% year-over-year. This was propelled by record vehicle deliveries of 512,000 units—up 45% from 353,000 units last year—across our flagship lineup. The Vanguard Apex SUV, our volume leader, delivered 285,000 units with an average selling price of $52,000, benefiting from price stabilization after targeted incentives in the US and China. Our new entry-level Vanguard Pulse hatchback, launched in Q2, ramped to 112,000 units, capturing share in the sub-$35,000 segment against competitors like BYD's Seagull and Chevy's Equinox EV.

Energy generation and storage revenue hit a milestone at $4.1 billion, up 62% year-over-year, representing 14% of total revenue—our fastest-growing segment. We deployed 6.2 GWh of storage products, including 3.8 GWh of Megavolt Packs for utility-scale projects and 1.5 GWh of home PowerCore units. Key wins included a 2 GWh deal with Southern California Edison, and average selling prices held firm at $320 per kWh thanks to vertical integration in LFP cathode production. This segment's gross margin soared to 28.2%, outpacing automotive as we leverage shared silicon carbide inverter technology across both businesses.

Services and other revenue contributed $1.0 billion, up 18% year-over-year, fueled by a 55% increase in Full Autonomy Miles Driven to 1.2 billion miles on our Vanguard Autonomy software—now at Level 3 certification in Texas and California. Regulatory credit sales added $450 million, primarily ZEV credits to legacy OEMs like GM and Ford.

Regionally, performance was well-balanced. North America drove 48% of revenue at $13.6 billion, up 35% year-over-year, boosted by IRA Section 30D credits averaging $7,500 per vehicle and our new Texas Gigafactory hitting a 250,000-unit annualized run-rate on the Apex line. Demand remains strong, with Q3 order backlog at 420,000 units. China contributed 28% or $7.9 billion, up 42% year-over-year, as we gained 2.2 points of share to 8.5% in the BEV segment. Localized production at Shanghai Gigafactory 2 avoided US tariff escalations, and partnerships with CATL on sodium-ion batteries for the Pulse addressed supply constraints amid trade frictions. Europe was 18% at $5.1 billion, up 22% year-over-year, tempered by softer demand post-subsidy cuts in Germany, but our Berlin plant's ramp to 150,000 units per year on the Vanguard Ridge semi-truck positions us for rebound as EU CO2 standards tighten in 2025. Rest of World rounded out at 6%, with early traction in Australia and Southeast Asia.

To give more granularity on our delivery performance, we achieved a record 512,000 vehicles globally, representing strong growth driven by production ramps and incentives. By model, the Apex SUV led with 285,000 units or about 56% of mix, up significantly year-over-year on range improvements and gigacasting efficiencies. The Pulse hatchback contributed 112,000 units, ramping quickly in entry-level segments. Trucks and premium models like the Ridge added the balance, with emerging semi-truck pre-orders bolstering the pipeline.

Geographically, North America was 58% of volume with over 295,000 units, Europe 20%, China 14%, and APAC ex-China plus rest of world the remainder, reflecting our U.S.-centric integration while expanding globally. Inventory levels are lean at under 20 days, with production utilization at 92% across gigafactories.

Turning to battery costs per kWh, a critical lever for profitability—batteries represent 35-40% of our vehicle bill of materials for models like the Apex SUV and Pulse. In Q3, our average battery pack cost was $92 per kWh, down 21% year-over-year from $116 per kWh and 5% sequentially from Q2's $97 per kWh. This positions us ahead of industry averages around $125 per kWh. Cells are at $78 per kWh at the module level. Over five years, we've reduced costs nearly 41% from $156 per kWh, targeting $70 per kWh by end-2026 via learning curves.

Fueling this are scale—we've produced over 15 GWh cumulatively—and vertical integration, eliminating outsourcing markups with our Panasonic JV on tabless 4680 cells. We've shifted 65% of volume to LFP chemistries at $65-70 per kWh, incorporating dry electrode coating for 30% solvent savings and silicon-dominant anodes for density gains. Regionally, China leads at $55-65 per kWh, but U.S. IRA credits make our Nevada output competitive at $90 per kWh, with dual-sourcing for Europe.

These savings contributed 320 basis points to automotive gross margin expansion. We've hedged lithium exposure—spot prices down 70% to $12,000 per ton—and invested in solid-state R&D for $50 per kWh by 2030.

On raw material costs and supply chain disruptions, these added pressure but we navigated better than peers. Raw materials contributed to some gross margin compression earlier, but Q3 stabilization via hedging preserved upside. Lithium prices moderated to $14,500 per ton, still elevated, impacting NMC cathodes at 15% higher costs, while nickel rose 35% to $18,500 per ton due to quotas. Aluminum and steel inflated 12% and 8%, semiconductors 10%. Disruptions like Red Sea rerouting delayed deliveries by weeks, inflating logistics 28%.

Mitigations included 70% take-or-pay contracts for 2025-2026 lithium and nickel at 15-20% below spot, shifting 40% to LFP slashing metal reliance, and recycling recovering 95% of materials. Gigafactory expansions localize 50% of cathodes, with AI inventory cutting stockouts. This recovered 60% of inflation via 7% ASP hikes, positioning margins for 25%+ expansion.

Regarding pricing strategies and promotions, our dynamic model and 'Accelerate' campaign drove 45% delivery growth while holding blended ASP steady. We cut Prime-like models 7% in NA to IRA thresholds, offered $4,500 rebates and low APR leases boosting U.S. leases 42%, bundled charging credits in Europe, and trade-ins in China. This shifted mix to high-volume models, reduced inventory 22%, turned FCF positive, and grew LTV 8%. NA saw 48% growth, Europe 15%, China stable in premium.

Our outlook for Q4 is total revenue of $29.5 to $31.0 billion, with automotive deliveries of 550,000-570,000 units. Full-year 2024 revenue now $112-115 billion, up 32-35%. Risks like policy shifts are mitigated by localization.

Next, I'll hand the call over to Raj Singh for an update on our manufacturing operations.

Raj Singh:
Thank you, Michael. Our manufacturing facilities are operating at peak efficiency to meet growing demand. Gigafactories in Nevada, Texas, Shanghai, and Berlin have hit high utilization, with Texas reaching 450,000 annualized run-rate on Apex lines through lean principles, automated stacking, and gigacasting reducing body-in-white costs 20%. We've implemented dry electrode pilots yielding 98%, cut lead times, and scaled to 100 GWh battery run-rate. Supply chain resilience via dual-sourcing and 85% vertical integration positions us to ramp further as backlog builds.

Following me, Dr. Lisa Novak will provide insights into our technological advancements.

Dr. Lisa Novak:
Thank you, Raj. We continue to invest heavily in R&D—over $2 billion this quarter—to maintain our edge. Advancements in battery tech include LFP with ApexShield coating for stability, 4680 tabless cells at 280 Wh/kg, silicon anodes, and sodium-ion pilots. Autonomy progress features Level 3 certification on 1.2 billion FAMD, neural nets trained on fleet data, and V4 Supercharger integration. Energy storage leverages shared inverters for Megavolt deployments. Solid-state with partners eyes 400 Wh/kg. These innovations drive range to 510 miles, towing to 14,000 lbs, and position us for robotaxi in 2025.

Now, I'll hand the call back to the operator for the Q&A session.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. Our first question comes from John Miller with Goldman Sachs.

Analyst 1:
Thanks, and congrats on the strong quarter. Michael, could you elaborate more on the battery cost trajectory and how regional differences factor into your $70 per kWh target by 2026?

Michael Reyes:
Thanks, John. Absolutely, our $92 per kWh in Q3 reflects accelerated declines via LFP shift to 65% volume, dry coating slashing solvents 30%, and scale from 15 GWh cumulative. China's $55-65 per kWh benchmark informs our CATL offtakes at $68 floors, U.S. IRA narrows gaps with Nevada at $90 qualifying fully, Europe dual-sourced for compliance. Hedging lithium at 5% COGS exposure and silicon pilots ensure we hit $70 by 2026, unlocking 28% margins.

Operator:
Next question from Emily Chen at Morgan Stanley.

Analyst 2:
Great, thanks. On raw materials and supply chain, how did disruptions specifically impact Q3 deliveries, and what's the hedge coverage looking forward?

Elena Vasquez:
Thanks, Emily. Disruptions like Red Sea added $1,200 per container and 5-week delays on 40% Asian shipments, plus border clogs inflating drayage 40%, totaling $320 per vehicle headwind. But our 70% take-or-pay for lithium/nickel through 2026 at discounts, LFP pivot cutting cobalt/nickel 60%, and localization from 65% Asia to 35% derisked us—margins beat consensus by 300 bps. Panama dredging and port pacts ease Q4 risks.

Operator:
Our next question from David Patel with JPMorgan.

Analyst 3:
Raj, manufacturing-wise, how are you scaling for Q4 guidance amid any lingering disruptions?

Raj Singh:
David, thanks. Our gigafactories are at 92% utilization, with Texas Phase 2 60% complete localizing cathodes, dry electrode at 98% yield boosting lines 20% faster. AI optimization cut stockouts to 2.5%, recycling offsets 8% lithium. We're confident ramping to 550-570k deliveries, with lean throughput improvements reducing lead times further.

Operator:
Next from Laura Kim at Barclays.

Analyst 4:
Lisa, impressive autonomy miles—how does this tie into delivery mix and monetization?

Dr. Lisa Novak:
Thanks, Laura. 1.2 billion FAMD drove 12-15% attach on Full Autonomy Package, adding $4,500 ASP premium and Level 3 in key states. OTA retraining on 2.5 billion miles hits 95% uptime, boosting high-utilization customer retention and services revenue 55%. Ties to 72% SUV/truck mix with FAP standard on premiums, paving robotaxi path.

Sarah Chen:
Thank you for your questions. We have time for two more.

Operator:
Our next question from Mark Thompson with Citi.

Analyst 5:
Elena, on deliveries by region and model, China was soft relatively—any pricing details there, and Q4 outlook?

Elena Vasquez:
Mark, China deliveries grew 42% revenue-wise to 8.5% share despite price wars, with Model Y-like Apex at RMB 229,900 countering BYD via LFP localization. Promotions like RMB 10k trade-ins grew premium share. Q4 targets recovery with 4680 transition, Baidu L4 trials—expecting 14-20% of total volume.

Operator:
Final question from Sophia Lee at UBS.

Analyst 6:
Michael, pricing and promotions clearly worked—how sustainable with inventory low, and margin implications?

Michael Reyes:
Sophia, our NovaAI engine and Accelerate campaign—rebates, leases, bundles—drove 45% volume at resilient 19-22% margins, LTV up 8% via subscriptions. Inventory at 18-52 days freed capital. Q4 ASP stabilizes at $47-52k, raw cost favorability adds 250 bps; targeting 25%+ GM with floors protecting long-term.

Operator:
Thank you. I would now like to turn the call back to Elena Vasquez for closing remarks.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us today. We are excited about the opportunities ahead—Q4 ramps, full-year beats, and our ecosystem momentum—and remain committed to creating long-term value for our shareholders. We look forward to sharing our progress with you next quarter.

Sarah Chen:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes the Vanguard Electric Vehicles Q3 2024 earnings call. You may now disconnect.
